title: Lottery Winners and Accident Victims
text:
In the 1970s Philip Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman interviewed three groups of people in Illinois. The first were recent winners of large prizes in the state lottery, sums ranging from fifty thousand dollars to a million. The second were people who had been paralyzed in accidents within the past year. The third were neighbors of the lottery winners, chosen as a comparison group.

All were asked how happy they were now, how happy they had been before, and how happy they expected to be in a couple of years. They also rated how much pleasure they got from everyday things, such as talking with a friend, watching television, eating breakfast, hearing a funny joke or getting a compliment.

The lottery winners were not significantly happier than the comparison group. And they took noticeably less pleasure in ordinary daily activities. The researchers suggested two reasons: once winning became the new standard, everyday pleasures looked smaller, and the thrill of the win itself faded with time. The accident victims rated their current happiness lower than the others, but still above the midpoint of the scale, higher than many people would have predicted.

The study became a classic illustration of hedonic adaptation: people adjust to good and bad fortune, returning to something near their usual level of happiness more than they expect. Later, larger studies found that some events, such as severe disability, do leave lasting effects, so adaptation is strong but not complete.
lesson: Do not bet your happiness on one big change, good or bad. People adapt to windfalls and to misfortune more than they expect, while daily pleasures and relationships keep mattering.
people: Philip Brickman, Dan Coates, Ronnie Janoff-Bulman
source: Brickman, P., Coates, D., and Janoff-Bulman, R. (1978). Lottery winners and accident victims: Is happiness relative? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 36(8), 917-927.
caveat: The samples were small (a few dozen people per group), and later large studies found that adaptation to severe disability is often incomplete.
